title: Time, Coordination, and Consensus

weeks.focus: Model and freeze physical-time assumptions, causal order, safety, liveness, failure detection, and consensus boundaries
Build persistent elections, replicated-log commitment, and deterministic state-machine application
Break leadership, clients, leases, snapshots, and membership, then diagnose invariant failures
Decide, migrate, operate, teach, evaluate, and remediate coordination choices
evidence: Security, cost, migration, ownership, and reversal plan

readiness_note: Review until teaching, lab, paired trials, calibration, semantic review, resource verification, focused validation, and full-course validation pass.

outcomes.statement: Calculate physical-clock drift, skew, and uncertainty and diagnose conclusions that exceed the available clock contract.
Derive happened-before, Lamport-clock, and vector-clock relationships without treating display order as causality.
Separate safety, liveness, and failure-detector assumptions and select consensus only for properties that require agreement.
Implement and diagnose Raft elections, persistent hard state, log matching, commitment, and state-machine application.
Implement client deduplication and linearizable reads with explicit ambiguous-outcome and quorum barriers.
Protect snapshots, membership changes, leases, and external resources with atomic state, overlapping quorums, and fencing.
Diagnose eight coordination failures from immutable same-input evidence and scoped safety oracles.
Defend a coordination architecture covering alternatives, operating limits, security, cost, migration, ownership, dissent, and reversal evidence.

resources.title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System
resources.author_or_publisher: Leslie Lamport; Communications of the ACM
resources.purpose: Derive happened-before, logical-clock rules, total-order limits, and explicit physical-clock assumptions.
resources.assignment: Read pages 558–563; construct one happened-before graph and identify two concurrent events that a scalar timestamp cannot distinguish.

resources.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
resources.author_or_publisher: James C. Corbett et al.; Google and USENIX OSDI
resources.purpose: Study a production system that exposes clock uncertainty instead of assuming perfect wall time.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 3 and 4.1–4.2; write the uncertainty interval, wait condition, guarantee, and infrastructure assumptions.

resources.title: Paxos Made Simple
resources.author_or_publisher: Leslie Lamport; Microsoft Research and ACM SIGACT
resources.purpose: Expose the single-value safety invariant behind quorum agreement and compare it with a replicated log.
resources.assignment: Read the complete paper; produce an acceptor promise/accepted-value ledger and one counterexample prevented by P2b.

resources.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm
resources.author_or_publisher: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout; USENIX ATC
resources.purpose: Connect elections, log replication, safety, clients, snapshots, and membership to explicit Raft properties.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 2–8; trace election safety, log matching, leader completeness, and state-machine safety through one leader change.

resources.title: Designing for Understandability: The Raft Consensus Algorithm
resources.purpose: Rehearse the visual event sequence for elections, log repair, and the five named safety properties.
resources.assignment: Watch 00:00–35:00 or read official slides 3–20; narrate one election and one conflicting-log repair without using architecture labels alone.

resources.title: Formal TLA+ Specification for the Raft Consensus Algorithm
resources.purpose: Map implementation state to formal variables and invariants without requiring prior TLA+ fluency.
resources.assignment: Read README and the state-variable, TypeOK, and state-machine-safety portions of raft.tla; map five variables to lab evidence and name one omitted liveness claim.

resources.title: The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely-Coupled Distributed Systems
resources.author_or_publisher: Mike Burrows; Google and USENIX OSDI
resources.purpose: Study operated leases, sequencers, caching, client behavior, and the gap between intended and actual use.
resources.assignment: Read Sections 2–5; record one lease assumption, one fencing/sequencer obligation, one cache risk, one operational limit, and the responsible owner.
